title: Static electricity: why a rubbed balloon sticks to the wall, and what lightning is

summary.text: Rub a balloon on dry hair, and your hair rises up towards it. Everything is made of tiny particles with electric charge, plus and minus, in equal amounts. Rubbing moves some of the tiny minus particles, called electrons, from your hair onto the balloon. Now the balloon has extra minus charge and your hair has extra plus charge, and opposite charges attract. Charge that stays where it was put is called static electricity. Lightning is the same thing on a giant scale: a huge spark that jumps when a storm cloud holds too much charge.
summary.art: A girl lifting a rubbed balloon slowly away from her head, her hair rising up towards it, with a storm cloud and a lightning bolt seen through the window behind her.

intro.hook: Rub a balloon on your hair, or on a woollen shawl, about ten times. Now hold it against the wall and let go. It stays there, with no tape and no glue. What is holding it up?
intro.text: Nothing you can see is holding the balloon. The rubbing has given it an electric charge, and the charge attracts the wall. In this unit you rub balloons, combs and rulers with different cloths, and find out which ones work best. You make paper jump, water bend and an empty can roll without touching them. You find out why it all works badly on a damp monsoon day. And you learn how a storm cloud does the same thing until it makes lightning, and how to stay safe when it does.
intro.art: A blue balloon stuck to a painted wall at a child's head height, with no tape, and a child's hand just letting go of it.

outcomes: I can explain that everything is made of tiny particles with plus and minus charge, in equal amounts, and that rubbing moves electrons from one thing to another.
I can say that opposite charges attract and the same charges repel, and use this to explain why my hair rises to a rubbed balloon and why the strands spread apart.
I can explain why a charged balloon attracts things that have no charge, like paper bits, a wall or a stream of water.
I can carry out a fair test of which cloth charges a balloon best, count my results, and say what I think, what I saw and why.
I can explain why static electricity works badly in damp air, and why a steel spoon held in my hand does not stay charged.
I can explain that lightning is a giant spark from a charged storm cloud, and that thunder is the sound of air heated by it.
I can say the rules for staying safe in a thunderstorm, and why each one helps.
I can tell how Thomas-François Dalibard and Benjamin Franklin showed that lightning is electricity.

terms.meaning: Something that tiny particles carry, which makes them push or pull on each other. It comes in two kinds, plus and minus.
terms.example: A rubbed balloon has extra minus charge, so it attracts your hair.
terms.art: A balloon with small minus signs on one side, and strands of hair with small plus signs rising towards it.

terms.meaning: One of the tiny particles that everything is made of. It is far too small to see, even with a strong magnifying glass.
terms.example: A single hair is a few hundred thousand atoms thick.
terms.art: A zoomed-in circle on a hair, showing round atoms packed side by side.

terms.meaning: A very tiny particle in the outer part of every atom. Every electron has a minus charge. Electrons are the part of an atom that can be rubbed off.
terms.example: When you rub a balloon on dry hair, some electrons move from your hair onto the balloon.
terms.art: An atom drawn as a small centre with tiny dots marked minus moving around it.

terms.meaning: A tiny particle in the centre of every atom. Every proton has a plus charge. Protons stay put in the atom and are not rubbed off.
terms.example: An atom with 6 protons and 6 electrons has no overall charge, because the plus and minus cancel.
terms.art: The centre of an atom, with small balls marked plus.

terms.meaning: Having the same amount of plus and minus charge, so that they cancel. Most things around us are neutral.
terms.example: A balloon straight out of the packet is neutral. It does not lift paper bits.
terms.art: A balloon with an equal number of small plus and minus signs scattered over it.

terms.meaning: Electric charge that has gathered on something and stays there. 'Static' means staying still. It is different from the moving charge in a wire.
terms.example: The charge on a rubbed balloon is static electricity. It can stay for many minutes on a dry day.
terms.art: A balloon stuck to a wall, with minus signs on the side touching the wall.

terms.meaning: To pull towards. Opposite charges, plus and minus, attract each other.
terms.example: A balloon with minus charge attracts your hair, which has plus charge.
terms.art: A minus sign and a plus sign with arrows pointing towards each other.

terms.meaning: To push away. Two of the same charge, two plus or two minus, repel each other.
terms.example: Hairs that all have plus charge repel each other and spread apart.
terms.art: Two plus signs with arrows pointing away from each other.

terms.meaning: A material that does not let charge move through it. Charge stays where it is put on an insulator.
terms.example: Rubber, plastic, wool and dry hair are insulators, so they can hold static charge.
terms.art: A plastic comb with minus signs staying in one patch near its teeth.

terms.meaning: A material that lets charge move through it easily. Metals, water and your body are conductors.
terms.example: A steel spoon rubbed on wool does not stay charged in your hand, because the charge runs through the steel and through you.
terms.art: A steel spoon held in a hand, with small arrows running from the spoon into the hand.

terms.meaning: Having a lot of water vapour in the air. Humid air makes things feel sticky and damp.
terms.example: Chennai in the monsoon is humid. Static tricks work badly then.
terms.art: A window with misty glass and a child fanning their sweaty face.

terms.meaning: A tiny flash and snap when charge jumps across air from one thing to another.
terms.example: Pulling off a sweater in a dark, dry room can make tiny sparks you can see and hear.
terms.art: A tiny blue spark jumping between a fingertip and a steel door handle.

terms.meaning: A giant spark between a storm cloud and the ground, or between two parts of a cloud.
terms.example: In April and May, evening storms bring lightning to Kerala and Karnataka.
terms.art: A bright branching lightning bolt from a dark cloud to the ground.

terms.meaning: The loud sound made when lightning heats the air so fast that the air bursts outwards.
terms.example: You see the flash first and hear the thunder after, because light travels much faster than sound.
terms.art: A lightning bolt with curved lines spreading out from it to show sound.

terms.meaning: A metal rod on top of a tall building, joined by a thick metal strip to the ground. Lightning goes down the strip instead of through the building.
terms.example: Tall apartment blocks and mobile phone towers usually have a lightning conductor on top.
terms.art: A tall building with a pointed rod on its roof and a metal strip running down its side into the ground.

terms.meaning: The space around a charged thing where it can push or pull other charges, without touching them.
terms.example: Bees can feel the electric field around a flower with the tiny hairs on their body.
terms.art: A charged balloon with faint lines spreading out from it into the air around.

explanations.definition: Every atom has a centre with plus charges, called protons, and minus charges around it, called electrons. In most things, there are exactly as many of each, so the charges cancel.
explanations.description: You, the balloon, the wall and the air are all made of atoms. Every atom holds plus charge in its centre and minus charge in its electrons. So a balloon straight from the packet is packed with charge. But it holds exactly as much plus as minus. The pushes and pulls cancel out, so it does nothing. We call it neutral. Things only start to push and pull when the balance is upset, when one thing has a few more electrons than it should, or a few fewer.
examples: A new balloon is neutral. Hold it over paper bits, and none jump.
A single grain of salt holds more electrons than there are people on Earth, and as many protons, so it is neutral.
Your body is neutral most of the time, though it is full of charge.
explanations.art: A balloon with a zoomed-in circle showing atoms, each with a plus centre and minus electrons, and a label 'plus and minus in balance'.
explanations.context: This card is about the charge hidden inside everything, and why most things show no sign of it.

explanations.definition: When two different materials rub together, some electrons move from one to the other. One ends up with extra minus charge, and the other with the same amount of extra plus charge.
explanations.description: Rubbing does not make charge. It only moves electrons. Some materials hold on to their electrons loosely, like hair, wool and glass. Others grab electrons, like rubber and many plastics. Rub a rubber balloon on dry hair, and electrons move from the hair to the balloon. The balloon now has extra minus charge. The hair has lost the same number of electrons, so it has extra plus charge. Rub two pieces of the same material together, and hardly any electrons move, because neither grabs harder. On an insulator like a balloon, the charge stays on the patch you rubbed. Turn the balloon round, and the other side does not lift paper.
examples: A plastic comb pulled through dry hair takes electrons from the hair.
A plastic ruler rubbed on a woollen sweater takes electrons from the wool.
Some materials give electrons to a balloon instead, such as a thin plastic carry bag. The balloon is charged either way.
explanations.art: A balloon being rubbed on hair, with a zoomed-in circle showing tiny minus dots moving from a hair onto the balloon's surface.
explanations.context: What actually happens when you rub a balloon on your hair? This card explains.

explanations.concept: Opposite charges attract, the same charges repel
explanations.definition: Plus and minus charges attract each other. Two plus charges repel each other, and so do two minus charges. The closer they are, the stronger the push or pull.
explanations.description: After rubbing, your hair has plus charge and the balloon has minus charge. Opposites attract, so the hairs rise up towards the balloon. Each hair also has plus charge, and so do the hairs next to it. The same charges repel, so the hairs push away from each other and stand apart, like a fan. That is why rubbed hair looks fly-away. The forces grow quickly as things get closer. Lift the balloon a little, and the hair still follows. Lift it far away, and the hair falls back down.
examples: Rubbed hair stands up and spreads out, each strand pushing the next away.
Strips of a plastic bag rubbed with wool spread out like a fan.
Two rubbed balloons hung side by side lean away from each other.
explanations.art: A child's hair standing up towards a balloon, with plus signs on the hairs, minus signs on the balloon, and small arrows between the hairs pointing apart.
explanations.context: Why does hair rise to a balloon, and why do the hairs spread apart? This card explains the rule for charges.

explanations.concept: Why a charged balloon attracts things with no charge
explanations.definition: A charged thing attracts a neutral thing by pushing or pulling the charges inside it a tiny way, so the near side gets the opposite charge.
explanations.description: A paper bit is neutral. So why does it jump up to a rubbed balloon? The balloon's extra minus charge pushes the electrons in the paper a tiny way back. Now the side of the paper nearest the balloon has a little more plus charge, and the far side a little more minus. The near side is pulled, and the far side is pushed. But the near side is closer, so its pull is stronger. The paper is pulled up overall. A wall, a stream of water and an empty can are attracted in the same way. The thing must be light, because the force is small. A paper bit jumps, but a book does not move.
examples: A rubbed balloon sticks to a painted wall.
A rubbed comb bends a thin stream of tap water.
A rubbed balloon rolls an empty can along the floor without touching it.
explanations.art: A paper bit under a balloon, with plus signs crowded on the top of the paper nearest the balloon, minus signs on its bottom, and an arrow pointing up.
explanations.context: A paper bit has no charge, but it still jumps to a rubbed balloon. This card explains why.

explanations.concept: Why static fails on a damp day
explanations.definition: Water lets charge move. In humid air, a very thin layer of water forms on surfaces, and the charge leaks away through it.
explanations.description: Static electricity needs the charge to stay put. On a dry day, a rubbed balloon can stay charged for a long time. On a humid day, a very thin layer of water forms on the balloon, too thin to see. Water is a conductor, so the extra electrons slowly leak away into the air and onto your hands. That is why static tricks work well in a dry Bengaluru or Delhi winter, and badly in a sticky Chennai or Kochi monsoon. An air-conditioned room helps, because an AC takes water out of the air. Your body is a conductor too. A steel spoon rubbed on wool does not stay charged while you hold it, because the charge runs through the steel and through you.
examples: Static shocks from a car door or a metal railing are common in dry winters, and rare in the monsoon.
Clean, dry hair charges well. Damp or oiled hair often charges badly.
A rubbed comb that touches the water stream stops bending it, because the wet comb loses its charge.
explanations.art: Two balloons side by side: one on a dry day with many paper bits clinging, one on a rainy day with water drops on the window and no paper bits.
explanations.context: Why do balloon tricks work some days and not others? This card explains what water in the air does to static charge.

explanations.definition: When enough charge builds up, it can jump across a gap of air to a conductor. The jump heats the air so fast that it glows and snaps. That is a spark.
explanations.description: Air is an insulator, so usually charge cannot cross it. But when a lot of charge builds up close to a conductor, the push gets strong enough to tear electrons off the atoms of the air. For a moment, a thin line of air carries the charge across. It gets very hot and glows. That is the flash. The heated air expands with a snap. That is the crackle. You may feel it as a small sting, called a static shock. A static shock from a sweater or a car door is not dangerous, because only a small amount of charge moves. Mains electricity is different. It keeps pushing, and it can kill.
examples: Pulling off a sweater in a dark room on a dry night makes tiny crackling sparks.
Touching a metal door handle after walking on a carpet can give a small shock.
Pulling a woollen blanket off a bed on a dry winter night can make it crackle.
explanations.art: A dark room with a child pulling a sweater over their head, and tiny blue sparks along the sweater.
explanations.context: Where do the crackles and tiny sparks of static come from? This card explains.

explanations.concept: How a storm cloud gets its charge
explanations.definition: A storm cloud gets charged as tiny ice crystals and soft bits of hail bump into each other inside it. Scientists agree on this much, but they still study exactly how each bump moves the charge.
explanations.description: A storm cloud can be more than 10 kilometres tall. Strong winds carry water drops up into the cold top of the cloud, where they freeze. Inside, tiny ice crystals and heavier soft hail, called graupel, crash into each other millions of times. Each bump moves a little charge from one to the other, like rubbing a balloon. The light ice crystals get plus charge and are carried up to the top of the cloud. The heavy graupel gets minus charge and stays lower down. So the cloud ends up with plus charge at the top and minus charge near the bottom. When the charge is big enough, a spark jumps. That spark is lightning.
examples: Most lightning jumps inside a cloud or between clouds, and never reaches the ground.
In India, lightning is most common just before and during the monsoon.
Lightning flashes about 40 to 50 times every second, somewhere on Earth.

perspectives.explanation: The main cause is bumping between ice crystals and graupel. Laboratory tests and measurements inside clouds show that these bumps move charge, and which piece gets plus depends on the temperature and the water in the cloud.

Bumping is not the whole story. Rising and sinking air may also carry charge from the ground and the air into the cloud. And nobody yet knows exactly how the first spark starts, because the measured charge in clouds seems too small to tear the air.

explanations.art: A tall storm cloud cut open, with small ice crystals marked plus rising to the top and bigger hail bits marked minus near the bottom, and a lightning bolt below.
explanations.context: How does a cloud, made of water and ice, get enough charge to make lightning? This card explains, and says what is still being studied.

explanations.definition: Lightning is a giant spark that heats the air in its path to nearly 30,000 degrees Celsius in a tiny fraction of a second. Thunder is the sound of that air bursting outwards.
explanations.description: The minus charge at the bottom of a storm cloud attracts plus charge on the ground below. When the charge is big enough, a spark jumps across kilometres of air. It is the same kind of spark as the crackle from a sweater, only millions of times bigger. The air in its path gets about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun. It glows white, and that is the flash. The hot air bursts outwards so fast that it makes a huge bang, and that is the thunder. Light reaches you almost at once, but sound takes about 3 seconds to travel 1 kilometre. So you see the flash first and hear the thunder later.
examples: A crackle from a sweater is a tiny flash and a tiny thunder.
A rumble of thunder is the sound from different parts of a long bolt arriving one after another.
Lightning tends to strike tall, pointed things, like trees, towers and poles.
explanations.art: A lightning bolt from a cloud to a hilltop, with a zoomed-in circle showing glowing hot air spreading outwards.
explanations.context: What is the flash, and what is the bang? This card explains lightning and thunder.

explanations.definition: Lightning can kill. The safest place in a thunderstorm is inside a building or a closed car with a metal roof.
explanations.description: In recent years, lightning has killed more than 2,000 people in India every year, more than any other force of nature. Most were outdoors, in fields, under trees or near water. Lightning strikes tall things and looks for an easy path to the ground. A person standing in an open field, or under a lone tree, can be that path. So when you hear thunder, go indoors at once and stay there until about 30 minutes after the last thunder. Inside, keep away from taps, bathing and corded appliances, because lightning can travel along pipes and wires. A closed car is safe because of its metal body, not its rubber tyres. Never fly a kite in a storm. India's weather scientists made a free phone app called Damini that warns when lightning is near.
examples: A family on a terrace goes indoors at the first rumble of thunder.
A tall apartment block has a lightning conductor on its roof, joined to the ground.
A farmer caught in the open crouches low with feet together, away from trees, if there is no shelter at all.
explanations.art: A family hurrying in from a terrace as a storm cloud gathers, and a red cross over a person standing under a lone tree in a field.
explanations.context: This card gives the rules for staying safe in a thunderstorm, and the reason for each one.

explanations.definition: Some animals can sense electric fields, the space around a charged thing where it pushes and pulls other charges.
explanations.description: A bumblebee needs to find flowers that still have nectar, and not waste time on ones another bee has just emptied. A flying bee picks up a small plus charge from rubbing against the air. A flower usually has a small minus charge. When a bee lands, some of the charge moves, and the flower's electric field changes for a while. Scientists in Bristol showed in 2013 that bumblebees can feel this with the tiny hairs on their body, and learn which flowers to skip. The charge also helps pollen jump from the flower onto the bee. Young spiders have a problem too: they have no wings, but need to travel to new places. Many climb up high and let out silk threads. The Earth's electric field pulls on the charged threads, and helps lift the spiders into the air.
examples: A bee's charge pulls pollen grains across a small gap onto their body.
Young spiders can float for kilometres on silk threads, which is called ballooning.
Sharks and some fish sense the electric signals of the animals they hunt.
explanations.art: A fuzzy bumblebee hovering by a flower, with faint lines around the flower and tiny pollen grains jumping up to the bee's hairs.
explanations.context: Static charge is not only in balloons and clouds. This card is about animals who use electric fields to find food and to travel.

agreed.text: Everything is made of atoms, with plus charge in the centre and minus charge in the electrons. Most things have equal amounts, so they are neutral.
agreed.evidence: J. J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897, and Ernest Rutherford found the atom's centre in 1911. Experiments since then have shown this for every material tested.

agreed.text: Opposite charges attract, and the same charges repel.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can see it with rubbed balloons, hair and plastic strips. Charles-Augustin de Coulomb measured these forces carefully in the 1780s.

agreed.text: Rubbing does not make charge. It moves electrons from one material to another, so one gains exactly what the other loses.
agreed.evidence: When both rubbed things are measured, one always has as much extra plus charge as the other has extra minus. No experiment has ever found charge being made or destroyed.

agreed.text: Lightning is a giant electric spark.
agreed.evidence: In 1752, Thomas-François Dalibard in France drew sparks from a tall iron rod during a storm, as Benjamin Franklin had suggested. Scientists now measure lightning with instruments on the ground and on satellites.

agreed.text: Lightning is dangerous, and being inside a building or a metal-roofed car is the safest place in a storm.
agreed.evidence: Records of lightning deaths in India and around the world show that most victims were outdoors. Weather services everywhere give the same advice.

challenging.for: Before rubbing, the balloon does nothing. After rubbing, it lifts paper. It seems the rubbing created something new.
challenging.against: The electrons were already in your hair. Rubbing only moved some of them to the balloon. Your hair is left with exactly as much plus charge as the balloon has extra minus, which is why your hair rises to it.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that rubbing creates electric charge.

challenging.claim: A paper bit jumps to a balloon because the paper is charged too.
challenging.for: Charged things attract each other, so it seems both must be charged.
challenging.against: The paper was never rubbed, and it is neutral. The balloon pushes the electrons inside the paper a tiny way, so the near side is pulled more than the far side is pushed.
challenging.context: This card is about why a neutral thing is attracted to a charged one.

challenging.claim: Lightning never strikes the same place twice.
challenging.for: A strike seems so rare and random that it feels unlikely to happen twice in one spot.
challenging.against: Lightning strikes tall, pointed things again and again. The Empire State Building in New York is struck about 20 to 25 times in a year.
challenging.context: This card is about an old saying that is not true.

challenging.claim: The rubber tyres of a car keep you safe from lightning.
challenging.for: Rubber is an insulator, so it seems it would stop the lightning reaching the car.
challenging.against: Lightning has just jumped kilometres through air, so a few centimetres of rubber cannot stop it. A closed car is safe because its metal body carries the charge around the outside and into the ground. A scooter or an open jeep is not safe.
challenging.context: This card is about why a car is a safe place in a storm, and why the reason is not the tyres.

challenging.claim: Static electricity and the electricity in a wire are two different kinds of electricity.
challenging.who: A common idea, from the two different names
challenging.for: Static stays on a balloon and gives a small snap. Electricity in a wire flows all the time and runs a fan. They seem very different.
challenging.against: Both are electric charge, carried by the same electrons. Static is charge that stays in one place. In a wire, the charge moves round a loop. A spark is static charge moving for a moment, like a current.
challenging.context: This card is about whether static electricity is a different thing from the electricity in your home's wires.

big_questions.q: A new balloon is full of plus and minus charges, but it does nothing. Is a balance of forces the same as no forces at all?
big_questions.hint: Think about a tug of war where both teams pull equally hard. Is the rope doing nothing?

big_questions.q: Rubbing moved electrons from your hair to the balloon. How did the electrons know which way to go?
big_questions.hint: Think about which materials grab electrons and which let them go. What happened when you rubbed a balloon with another balloon?

big_questions.q: Why does the electric force hide so well, when it can lift your hair against the pull of the whole Earth?
big_questions.hint: Think about how much plus and minus charge there is in everything, and how exactly they cancel.

big_questions.q: Bees feel the electric field of a flower. What would the world feel like if you could sense electric fields too?
big_questions.hint: Think about the balloon, the storm cloud, your own body and the wires in the walls.

big_questions.q: People once thought lightning was thrown by gods. Today we know it is a spark. Does knowing how it works make lightning less wonderful, or more?
big_questions.hint: Think about how you felt when your own balloon made a tiny spark.

big_questions.q: Every atom in you holds plus and minus in balance. Are you, too, a kind of balance?
big_questions.hint: Think about what would happen to you if all your electrons were taken away.

story.title: Sparks in Thatha's Sweater
story.note: The story is made up. The science in it is true: in dry winter air, pulling off a woollen or synthetic sweater in the dark can make tiny sparks you can see and hear, and a balloon rubbed on wool attracts paper bits.
text: It was January in Bengaluru, and the nights were cold and dry. Revathi was nine. She lived in a flat on the fourth floor with her mother and her grandfather, Thatha. Thatha had come from Madurai for the winter, and he was not used to the cold. Every evening he wore his thick brown sweater, the one Revathi's mother had knitted for him.
One night the power went off just before bedtime. The fan stopped and the whole building went dark. Outside, the street lights were off too.
"I will go to bed anyway," said Thatha. "It is too cold to sit up." He stood in the dark in the middle of the room and pulled his sweater up over his head.
Crackle, crackle, snap.
Revathi saw it. Tiny blue flashes, like the smallest stars, ran along the wool as it came off. They were gone in a moment.
"Thatha! Your sweater is sparkling!"
Thatha froze with the sweater in his hands. "What do you mean, sparkling?"
"There were little blue lights on it. And it went crackle. Do it again."
Thatha laughed, but he pulled the sweater back on, and then pulled it off again, slowly. Crackle. This time he saw the sparks too, tiny and blue, running across the wool near his face.
"Ayyo," said Thatha. "Is it burning? Is it the wiring?" He held the sweater far away from him.
"It can't be the wiring," said Revathi. "The power is off. There is no electricity in the house at all."
"Then where do the sparks come from?" asked Thatha.

Revathi did not know. But she wanted to. She remembered something her mother had shown her last week. They had rubbed a balloon on Revathi's hair, and her hair had stood straight up towards it. Her mother had said the balloon had a charge on it. The rubbing had moved tiny particles called electrons from her hair onto the balloon.

"Thatha," she said slowly, "when you pull off the sweater, the wool rubs on your shirt. Maybe the rubbing moves electrons, like with the balloon. And then they jump back. Maybe the jump is the spark."
"You think so?" said Thatha.
"I can test it," said Revathi. "Tomorrow."

The next afternoon, the power was back. Revathi tore a paper napkin into twenty tiny bits and put them in a pile on the dining table. She took a balloon from the drawer and blew it up. Her mother tied it.
"First, a test with no rubbing," said Revathi. She held the balloon just above the paper bits. Nothing moved.
Then she rubbed the balloon on Thatha's brown sweater, ten times, quickly. She held it above the paper bits again. Pit, pit, pit. The bits jumped up and clung to the balloon. She counted. "Eleven!"
"So the sweater gives the balloon a charge," said her mother.

"Now the cotton towel," said Revathi. She patted the balloon all over with a damp hand, waited a minute, and checked that it lifted nothing. Then she rubbed it on the towel, ten times. Only two bits jumped.
"The wool works much better than the cotton," she said. "Wool must give away its electrons easily."
Thatha was watching closely now, his glasses pushed up on his forehead. "And the sparks?"

"They come when the electrons jump back," said Revathi. "The sweater and your shirt get opposite charges when they rub. Opposite charges attract. When enough charge builds up, it jumps across the air in a spark. That is the crackle. Amma, isn't it the same as lightning?"
Her mother nodded. "Lightning is the same thing, only very, very big. A storm cloud builds up charge, and then it jumps in one giant spark."
"So your sweater makes tiny lightning, Thatha," said Revathi. "And the crackle is tiny thunder."
Thatha looked at his sweater as if he had never seen it before. "Seventy-two years I have worn sweaters," he said. "And nobody ever told me I was making lightning."
That night, Revathi switched off the lights on purpose. Thatha stood in the middle of the dark room and pulled off his sweater, very slowly.
Crackle, snap. The tiny blue sparks ran across the wool.
"Tiny lightning," said Thatha, and he laughed so loudly that the neighbour's dog started to bark.

In March, when Thatha went home to Madurai, he told Revathi on the phone that his sweater had stopped sparkling. "It is the hot, damp air here," Revathi told him. "Water in the air lets the charge leak away before it can build up. Wait until next January, Thatha. Come back to Bengaluru, and your sweater will sparkle again."
story.epiphany: For the parent: rubbing two different materials moves electrons from one to the other. The wool and the shirt rub as the sweater comes off, so they get opposite charges. When enough charge builds up, it jumps across the air as a tiny spark, which glows and crackles. Lightning is the same kind of spark on a giant scale. Revathi's test also shows two things a scientist does: she tested the balloon first with no rubbing, and she took the old charge off before each new cloth, so the test was fair.
ask: Why did Revathi know the sparks were not coming from the wiring?
Why did she hold the balloon over the paper first, before rubbing it?
Why did she pat the balloon with a damp hand before rubbing it on the towel?
Which worked better, the wool or the cotton? What does that tell you about wool?
Why did the sweater stop sparkling in Madurai?

A girl pointing at the sweater in surprise, her grandfather holding it at arm's length.
A girl holding a balloon over a pile of torn paper napkin bits on a dining table, the bits leaping up to it, her grandfather watching with his glasses pushed up.
A grandfather laughing in a dark room as tiny sparks crackle on his sweater, and the girl laughing beside him.

games.title: Plus or Minus: the charge card game
games.context: This is a card game about charges. Two cards are turned over, and the first player to say whether they attract, repel or do nothing wins the pair.

printables.title: 30 charge cards to cut out
items: 8 PLUS cards: a rubbed hair, a rubbed woollen sweater, a rubbed glass bangle, the top of a storm cloud
8 MINUS cards: a rubbed balloon, a rubbed plastic comb, a rubbed plastic ruler, the bottom of a storm cloud
10 NEUTRAL cards: a paper bit, a wall, a stream of water, an empty can, a new balloon, a grain of pepper

printables.title: Answer card
items: PLUS or MINUS with NEUTRAL: attract, a little

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them face down in a pile.
The dealer turns over two cards, side by side.
The first player to say 'attract', 'repel' or 'nothing', correctly, wins both cards.
If someone says the wrong answer, the other players can win the pair by saying why it is wrong.
A SPARK! card: the player who turned it over explains how a spark happens, then takes 2 cards from the pile.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most cards wins.
Playing alone: turn over two cards, say your answer, and check it on the answer card. Try to get 12 right in a row.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Read the answer card together. 3. Shuffle the cards.
flow.say: Every card is plus, minus or neutral. When I turn two over, say what they do to each other. Attract, repel, or nothing.
flow.kid: Every card is plus, minus or neutral. Read the answer card first.
flow.context: This is the first step of Plus or Minus, a card game where you say what two charges do to each other.

flow.do: Play one practice pair together: a rubbed balloon and a paper bit.
flow.say: A rubbed balloon and a paper bit. The paper bit is neutral. Do they attract, repel, or do nothing?
flow.kid: A rubbed balloon and a paper bit. What happens? Tap your answer.

check.q: A rubbed balloon, with minus charge, meets a neutral paper bit. What happens?
options: Nothing, because the paper has no charge
They attract
They repel
check.why: They attract. The balloon pushes the electrons in the paper a tiny way back, so the near side of the paper has a little plus charge, and that side is pulled up. Picking 'nothing' is a good thought, because the paper has no extra charge. But a charged thing still attracts a neutral one.

flow.do: 1. Play until the pile is finished. 2. Count the cards each player won.
flow.say: Turn over two cards. Who can say it first? Remember to say why.
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. Say attract, repel or nothing. Then say why.
flow.parent: Ask for a reason now and then. A good reason for two minus cards: both have extra electrons, and the same charges push apart. For two neutral cards: the plus and minus in each cancel, so neither pushes or pulls.

flow.do: Talk about the storm cloud cards.
flow.say: The top of a storm cloud is plus. The bottom is minus. What do you think happens when the two get too much charge?
flow.kid: The cloud's top is plus. Its bottom is minus. What happens next?
flow.think: Why does lightning not happen all the time, if the top and bottom of a cloud attract?

setup.caption: 1. Turn over two cards.

setup.art: A child holding a small pile of won cards, and the answer card lying beside the pile.
setup.caption: 2. Say attract, repel or nothing first, and win the pair.

games.title: Storm Run: a board game about lightning safety
games.context: This is a board game. You race from a field to a safe house while a storm comes closer. Storm cards ask what you would do, and a safe answer moves you ahead.

printables.title: Storm Run board
items: A path of 24 squares from a paddy field to a house, passing a lone tree, a pond, a bus stop and a temple tank
Every third square is a STORM square with a cloud on it
The last square is HOME: inside a house with the door shut

printables.title: 16 storm cards
items: You hear thunder while playing cricket in the park. Go home at once, or finish the over? (Go home at once. If you can hear thunder, lightning can reach you.)
There is a big tree alone in the field. Shelter under it? (No. Lightning often strikes tall things standing alone.)
Your cousin wants to fly a kite as the clouds gather. Is that safe? (No. The wet string can carry lightning to her hand.)
You are inside during a storm. Is it a good time for a bath? (No. Lightning can travel along water pipes.)
You are in a closed car in a storm. Get out and run, or stay in? (Stay in. The metal body carries lightning round you to the ground.)
You are swimming in a temple tank and hear thunder. What do you do? (Get out of the water at once and go indoors.)
The thunder stopped five minutes ago. Go back out to play? (Not yet. Wait about 30 minutes after the last thunder.)
You are on an open scooter in a storm. Is it as safe as a car? (No. A scooter has no metal roof around you. Stop and go inside a building.)
You are caught in a field with no building near. What is safest? (Crouch low with your feet together, away from trees and poles.)
Amma's phone app Damini says lightning is near. What do you do? (Go indoors and stay in.)
During the storm, can you stand on the terrace to watch? (No. Watch from inside, away from the window.)
Your friend says lightning never strikes the same place twice. True? (No. Tall towers are struck many times a year.)
Lightning flashes and the thunder comes 3 seconds later. Is it far away? (No. It is about 1 kilometre away. Go in at once.)
You are under a bus stop with a thin metal roof and no walls. Is it a safe shelter? (No. Go inside a proper building.)
You see a fallen electric wire after the storm. Touch it? (Never. Stay away and tell a grown-up.)
You are indoors. Should you keep away from corded appliances and taps until the storm passes? (Yes. Lightning can travel along wires and pipes.)

printables.title: A counter for each player and one dice

rules: Everyone starts in the paddy field. Take turns to roll the dice and move.
Land on a STORM square: another player reads you a storm card.
Give the safe answer and say why: move ahead 2 squares. Give an unsafe answer: move back 2 squares.
The first player to reach HOME wins.
Playing alone: read the card, say your answer, then check the answer in the brackets.

flow.do: 1. Put the board on the table. 2. Put the storm cards face down. 3. Put all counters on the paddy field.
flow.say: A storm is coming. We are all out in a paddy field, and we must get home safely. The storm cards ask what you would do.
flow.kid: A storm is coming! Race from the field to home. Answer safely.
flow.context: This is the first step of Storm Run, a board game about staying safe from lightning.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to roll and move. 2. On a STORM square, read a card. 3. Ask for the reason, not only the answer.
flow.say: Roll and move. On a storm square, I will read you a card. Tell me what you would do, and why.
flow.kid: Roll and move. On a storm square, answer the card. Say why.

check.q: It starts to thunder while you are in an open field. There is one big tree near you. Where is safest?
options: Under the tree, out of the rain
Running to the nearest building, or crouching low away from the tree if there is none
Standing tall in the middle of the field
check.why: Lightning often strikes tall things standing alone, like a lone tree, and can jump from the tree to a person sheltering below. A building is safest. Picking 'under the tree' makes sense for rain, but not for lightning.

flow.do: Talk about the car card.
flow.say: A closed car is safe in a storm. Many people think it is because of the rubber tyres. What do you think keeps you safe?
flow.kid: A car is safe in a storm. Is it the tyres? Or something else?
flow.parent: The metal body of the car carries the charge round the outside and down to the ground. The tyres are far too thin to stop lightning, which has just crossed kilometres of air.

setup.caption: 1. Put everyone on the paddy field.

setup.caption: 2. Land on a storm square and answer safely to move ahead.

experiments.title: The Rubbing Test: which cloth charges a balloon best?
experiments.question: If you rub a balloon with different things, which one gives it the most charge? Does a balloon rubbed with another balloon get charged at all?
experiments.predict: Look at the things you will rub the balloon with: dry hair, a woollen sweater, a cotton towel, a newspaper and a second balloon. Which one will make the most paper bits jump up? Which will make the fewest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same balloon, the same 20 paper bits, the same 10 rubs and the same height every time. Only the thing you rub with changes. Before each new rub, take the old charge off the balloon, and check that it lifts no bits. Do each one twice, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: two round balloons, blown up and tied
a paper napkin or tissue, torn into 20 bits each about the size of your little fingernail. If the tissue has two layers, peel them apart first.
things to rub with: clean dry hair, a woollen sweater, shawl or monkey cap, a cotton towel, a sheet of newspaper
a ruler
a dark plate or a sheet of dark paper, so the paper bits are easy to see

experiments.safety: Pick up every piece of a popped balloon at once, because small children can choke on them. A grown-up blows up the balloons if the child finds it hard.

schedule.what: Guess, then rub a balloon with 5 different things and count the paper bits it lifts each time.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar for each thing you rubbed with, as tall as the number of bits it lifted.

flow.do: 1. Shut the windows. If you have an AC, run it for 30 minutes first. 2. Put the 20 paper bits in a small heap on the dark plate. 3. Hold the plain balloon 2 cm above them for 3 seconds.
flow.say: First, a test with no rubbing at all. Hold the balloon just above the paper. Watch closely. Does anything jump?
flow.kid: Hold the balloon just above the paper bits. Do any jump?
flow.parent: No bits should jump, because a new balloon is neutral. This is the starting test that every other result is compared with. Static works best in dry air. In the monsoon, or in Chennai or Kochi, an AC room helps a lot, because an AC takes water out of the air.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rubbing Test. Here you check that a balloon that has not been rubbed lifts no paper.

flow.do: 1. Show the five things: dry hair, wool, cotton, newspaper and the second balloon. 2. Ask your child to put them in order, from most bits to fewest. 3. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: We will rub the balloon with each of these, ten times. Which will make the most bits jump? Which the fewest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which thing will make the most bits jump? Which the fewest? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will work best?
good: Because the sweater made sparks in the story.
Because hair stood up to the balloon before.

flow.parent: Do not say what will happen. Any reason your child gives is good. It tells you what they think now.

flow.do: 1. Rub one side of the balloon 10 times on the first thing, firmly, in one direction. 2. Hold the rubbed side 2 cm above the heap for 3 seconds. 3. Count the bits that cling. 4. Pick off the bits. 5. Pat the balloon all over with a damp hand, wait one minute, and check it lifts no bits. 6. Go on to the next thing.
flow.say: Rub ten times on one side. Hold that side over the paper. Count the bits that stick. Then pat it with a damp hand to take the charge off.
flow.kid: Rub ten times. Hold it over the paper. Count the bits. Then pat it with a damp hand.
flow.parent: Hair, if it is clean, dry and not oiled, and wool usually lift the most bits. Cotton and newspaper usually lift fewer. A balloon rubbed with another balloon usually lifts very few or none, because both are the same material, so neither grabs electrons harder. Results vary from day to day, so a different order is fine, as long as you saw it. If nothing lifts at all, the air is too damp. Try in an AC room, make the bits smaller, or do the water-bending test instead, which works in damper air.

check.q: Why do we pat the balloon with a damp hand and check it before each new rub?
options: To clean off dust
To take away the old charge, so each result shows only the new rubbing
To warm up the balloon
check.why: Some charge from the last rub could still be on the balloon. Water and your hand are conductors, so patting takes the charge away, and the check shows it has gone. Then each count shows only what the new cloth did. Picking 'dust' is a sensible thought, but the charge is what matters here.

flow.do: 1. Rub one side of the balloon on wool. 2. Hold the other side, the side you did not rub, over the bits. 3. Then turn the rubbed side to the bits.
flow.say: Now a puzzle. I rub only this side. What will the other side do over the paper? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Rub one side only. Hold the other side over the paper. What happens?
flow.parent: The unrubbed side lifts few or no bits. The rubbed side lifts many. Rubber is an insulator, so the charge stays on the patch where it was put. That is why it is called static, which means staying still.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: some things give the balloon much more charge than others. What I saw: after wool it lifted 12 bits, after cotton only 3, and after the other balloon none. Why: rubbing moves electrons. Wool lets go of its electrons easily, and the balloon grabs them. Two balloons are the same material, so neither grabs harder.

check.q: A balloon rubbed with a second balloon lifted no paper bits. What is the best reason?
options: The second balloon was too soft
Both are the same material, so hardly any electrons moved from one to the other
Balloons cannot have charge
check.why: Electrons move when one material grabs them harder than the other does. Two balloons are made of the same rubber, so neither grabs harder, and hardly any charge moves. Picking 'balloons cannot have charge' does not fit, because the same balloon lifted many bits after it was rubbed on wool.

experiments.context: In this experiment you rub a balloon with five different things and count how many paper bits it lifts each time. You find out which ones charge it best.

setup.caption: 2. Rub 10 times with one thing.

experiments.title: Bend the Water: can every rubbed thing do it?
experiments.question: A rubbed plastic comb can bend a thin stream of water. Can a rubbed plastic ruler do it? Can a rubbed steel spoon?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will a comb that has not been rubbed bend the water? Will a rubbed ruler? Will a steel spoon rubbed on wool? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Keep the stream the same size the whole time. Rub each thing 10 times on the same dry hair or wool. Hold each one the same distance from the stream, about 1 cm, without touching the water.
results_table: A lot, a little or not at all?

materials.item: a kitchen or bathroom tap
a plastic comb
a plastic ruler or a plastic pen
a steel spoon
a woollen sweater or shawl, or clean dry hair
a towel to dry your hands

experiments.safety: Keep away from any switches or sockets near the tap. Dry your hands before you rub anything, and turn the tap off when you finish.

schedule.what: Make a thin stream of water. Bring an unrubbed comb, a rubbed comb, a rubbed ruler and a rubbed spoon close to it.

experiments.record: Draw the stream of water four times. Next to each, draw the thing you held near it, and show how much the water bent.

flow.do: 1. Open the tap slowly until the water runs in a thin, smooth stream, about as thick as a pencil lead. 2. Bring the comb, without rubbing it, close to the stream.
flow.say: First we need a very thin stream, as thin as a pencil lead. Now let's hold the comb near it, with no rubbing. What happens?
flow.kid: Make a very thin stream. Hold the comb near it. Does it bend?
flow.parent: The stream must be thin and smooth, not dripping. The unrubbed comb should not bend it. This is the starting test.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bend the Water. Here you make a thin stream from a tap and test a comb that has not been rubbed.

flow.do: 1. Dry your hands. 2. Comb dry hair 10 times fast, or rub the comb on wool. 3. Hold the comb about 1 cm from the stream, without touching it.
flow.say: Now rub the comb ten times. Bring it close to the water, but don't touch. Watch the stream. What do you think will happen? Why?
flow.kid: Rub the comb ten times. Hold it close. Don't touch the water!
flow.parent: The stream should bend towards the comb, often clearly, by a few millimetres or more. This works even on many days when balloons do not, because the water is so light and so close. If the comb touches the water, it gets wet and stops working. Dry it and rub again.

ask.q: The water has no charge. Why did it bend towards the comb?
good: The comb pulled the near side of the water.
The comb's charge pushed the water's electrons back, so the near side got pulled.

flow.do: 1. Rub the plastic ruler 10 times on wool. 2. Hold it 1 cm from the stream. 3. Now rub the steel spoon 10 times on wool, holding its handle. 4. Hold it 1 cm from the stream.
flow.say: Now the ruler. Then the steel spoon. The spoon is rubbed just as hard. Will it bend the water too?
flow.kid: Try the rubbed ruler. Then try the rubbed steel spoon. What happens?
flow.parent: The ruler bends the water like the comb. The steel spoon does not, however hard you rub it. Steel is a conductor. Any charge that moves onto it runs through the steel, through your hand and away through your body.

check.q: A rubbed comb bends the water, but a rubbed steel spoon does not. Why?
options: The spoon is too heavy
Steel is a conductor, so the charge runs through the spoon and into your hand
Spoons are not allowed near water
check.why: Plastic is an insulator, so the charge stays on the comb. Steel is a conductor, and so is your body. Any charge on the spoon runs away through your hand. Picking 'too heavy' is a fair guess, but the spoon does not move, only the water does, so the spoon's weight does not matter.

flow.do: 1. Rub the comb again. 2. Let it touch the stream for a moment. 3. Hold it near the stream again without drying it.
flow.say: Last test. Let the rubbed comb touch the water once. Now does it still bend the stream?
flow.kid: Let the comb touch the water once. Does it still work?
flow.parent: After touching the water, the wet comb bends the stream much less, or not at all. Water is a conductor, so the charge leaks away. This is also why static works badly on damp days.

flow.do: Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Now tell me what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: rubbed plastic can bend water, but rubbed metal cannot. What I saw: the comb and the ruler bent the stream, the unrubbed comb and the spoon did not, and the wet comb stopped working. Why: plastic is an insulator and keeps its charge. Steel and water are conductors, so the charge runs away.
flow.think: Your body is a conductor. So how can your hair stay charged after rubbing?

experiments.context: In this experiment you bring rubbed and unrubbed things close to a thin stream of water. You find out which ones bend it, and why a steel spoon does not.

activities.title: The Sticky Balloon and the Rising Hair

materials.item: a round balloon, blown up and tied
a woollen sweater, shawl or monkey cap, or clean dry hair
a mirror

activities.safety: Pick up every piece of a popped balloon at once, because small children can choke on them.

schedule.what: Rub a balloon and stick it to the wall. Then lift your hair with it in front of a mirror.

activities.record: Draw the balloon on the wall, and draw your hair rising up to the balloon.

flow.do: 1. Rub the balloon on dry hair or wool 10 times. 2. Press it gently against a painted wall and let go. 3. Try a plain balloon, not rubbed, the same way.
flow.say: Watch this. I rub the balloon and hold it on the wall. Now I let go. What do you notice? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Rub the balloon ten times. Hold it on the wall. Let go!
flow.parent: On a dry day the rubbed balloon often stays on the wall for many minutes. The plain balloon falls at once. On a damp day it may slide down after a few seconds. That is fine: it still shows the difference.
flow.context: This is a starting activity for static electricity. You stick a rubbed balloon to a wall with nothing but its charge.

flow.do: 1. Stand in front of the mirror. 2. Rub the balloon on your hair 10 times. 3. Lift it slowly upwards, about 5 cm above your head.
flow.say: Now rub the balloon on your hair, and lift it slowly. Watch your hair in the mirror. Why do you think the hair rises?
flow.kid: Rub the balloon on your hair. Lift it slowly. Look in the mirror!
flow.parent: Clean, dry, unoiled hair works best. If your child's hair is oiled, try someone else's, or use wool on the balloon and hold it near a forearm to see the tiny hairs lift.

ask.q: What do you think is pulling your hair up?
good: The rubbing did something to the balloon and the hair.

flow.do: Look at the hair closely.
flow.say: Look at the hairs. They rise to the balloon, but they also spread apart from each other. Why might that be?
flow.kid: Your hairs rise. They also spread apart. Why?

check.q: A plain balloon falls off the wall, but a rubbed one sticks. What did the rubbing change?
options: It made the balloon sticky
It gave the balloon an electric charge
It made the balloon lighter
check.why: Rubbing moved electrons onto the balloon, so it has an electric charge, and the charge attracts the wall. Picking 'sticky' is a natural first thought, but the balloon is not sticky to touch, and a plain balloon of the same rubber falls.

flow.think: If the hairs spread apart, what does that tell you about the charge on each hair?

activities.context: This is a quick activity to start the unit. You stick a balloon to a wall and lift your hair, using only the charge from rubbing.

setup.art: A child rubbing a balloon on a woollen shawl, then pressing it against a painted wall where it stays.
setup.caption: 1. Rub the balloon and stick it to the wall.

setup.art: A child in front of a mirror, lifting a balloon above their head, their hair rising and spreading towards it.
setup.caption: 2. Lift your hair with the balloon in a mirror.

activities.title: The Plastic Tassel: charges that push apart

materials.item: a thin plastic carry bag, the crinkly kind
scissors
cello tape
a woollen sweater, shawl or monkey cap, or clean dry hair

activities.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors.

schedule.what: Cut a plastic bag into a tassel of strips. Rub it with wool and watch the strips spread apart.

activities.record: Draw the tassel before rubbing and after rubbing. Mark the charge on each strip.

flow.do: 1. Cut a strip of the bag about 30 cm long and 10 cm wide. 2. Cut it into thin strips, about 1 cm wide, but leave 3 cm joined at the top. 3. Tape the top to the edge of a table, so the strips hang down.
flow.say: We are making a tassel of thin plastic strips. Look how they hang down together, all touching.
flow.kid: Cut the bag into thin strips. Leave the top joined. Hang it up.
flow.context: This activity shows that the same charges repel. You make a tassel of plastic strips and watch them push each other apart.

flow.do: 1. Hold the wool around the top of the tassel. 2. Pull it down the strips 5 or 6 times. 3. Let go and step back.
flow.say: Now we rub every strip in the same way. Before I let go, guess: will the strips stick together, or spread apart? Why?
flow.kid: Pull the wool down the strips five times. Let go. What happens?
flow.parent: The strips spread out into a fan, and push away from your hand too if you bring the wool near. Every strip got the same kind of charge from the wool, and the same charges repel. On a damp day the spread is smaller. Try again in an AC room.

check.q: The rubbed plastic strips spread apart. Why?
options: The wool blew air between them
Every strip has the same kind of charge, and the same charges repel
The strips got heavier
check.why: All the strips were rubbed with the same wool, so they all got the same kind of charge. The same charges push each other away. Picking 'air' is a good guess, but the strips stay spread out long after the wool has gone.

flow.do: Compare the tassel with rubbed hair.
flow.say: Remember your hair after the balloon? How is it like this tassel?
flow.kid: How is this tassel like your hair after the balloon?
flow.parent: Rubbed hairs each have the same plus charge, so they spread apart, just like the strips.

activities.context: In this activity you make a tassel of plastic strips, rub it with wool and watch the strips push each other apart.

setup.art: A tassel of thin plastic strips taped to a table edge, hanging straight down.
setup.caption: 1. Hang up a tassel of thin plastic strips.

setup.art: The same tassel after rubbing, its strips spread out wide like a fan.
setup.caption: 2. Rub it with wool and let go.

activities.title: Pepper Jumps, Salt Stays

materials.item: a round balloon, blown up and tied
a woollen sweater, shawl or monkey cap, or clean dry hair
half a teaspoon of ground black pepper and one teaspoon of salt, mixed on a dark plate

activities.safety: Pick up every piece of a popped balloon at once, because small children can choke on them. Do not breathe in the pepper, and wash your hands after.

schedule.what: Mix salt and pepper. Use a rubbed balloon to pick out the pepper.

activities.record: Draw the plate and the balloon. Show which grains jumped up.

flow.do: 1. Mix the salt and the pepper on the plate. 2. Ask: how could you get the pepper out without touching it?
flow.say: Here is salt and pepper, all mixed up. Can you think of a way to take the pepper out, without fingers or a spoon?
flow.kid: Salt and pepper are mixed up. How could you pick out the pepper?
flow.context: This activity uses a rubbed balloon to pick pepper out of salt. It shows how charge can lift tiny light grains, the way a bee picks up pollen.

flow.do: 1. Rub the balloon on wool 10 times. 2. Hold it about 2 cm above the plate. 3. Lower it slowly, and stop as soon as grains jump.
flow.say: Rub the balloon. Lower it slowly over the plate. Which grains jump first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Rub the balloon. Lower it slowly. Which grains jump first?
flow.parent: The black pepper usually jumps up first, because pepper grains are lighter than salt grains. If you go too low, the salt jumps too. If nothing jumps, the air may be too damp.

flow.do: Talk about bees.
flow.say: A bee needs pollen from flowers. A flying bee picks up a plus charge, and a flower has a small minus charge. What might happen to the pollen when a bee comes close?
flow.kid: A bee has charge, like your balloon. What happens to the pollen?

check.q: Why does the pepper jump up to the balloon before the salt does?
options: Pepper grains are lighter, so the small electric force can lift them first
Pepper is charged and salt is not
Salt is a magnet
check.why: The rubbed balloon attracts both pepper and salt. But the force is small, so the lighter pepper grains are lifted first. Picking 'pepper is charged' is a fair guess, but neither was rubbed: both are attracted because the balloon is charged.

flow.parent: Pollen grains jump across a small gap onto a charged bee, in the same way as the pepper. This helps the bee carry pollen, and helps the plant spread their pollen to other flowers.

activities.context: In this activity you use a rubbed balloon to pick pepper out of salt, and find out how bees use charge to collect pollen.

setup.caption: 1. Mix salt and pepper on a dark plate.

setup.art: A rubbed balloon held just above the plate, with black pepper grains leaping up to it and the white salt staying behind.
setup.caption: 2. Lower a rubbed balloon slowly. Watch the pepper jump.

activities.title: Sparks in the Dark

materials.item: a woollen or synthetic sweater, or a fleece blanket
a round balloon, blown up and tied
a room you can make fully dark at night

activities.safety: Pick up every piece of a popped balloon at once, because small children can choke on them. Never do this near a gas stove or anything that can catch fire.

schedule.what: In a fully dark room, pull off a sweater slowly, and watch and listen for tiny sparks.

activities.record: Write what you heard and what you saw. Draw the sparks.

flow.do: 1. At night, switch off every light and close the curtains. 2. Wait one minute, so your eyes get used to the dark.
flow.say: We are going to look for tiny lightning. First our eyes must get used to the dark. Let's wait a whole minute.
flow.kid: Turn off the lights. Wait one minute in the dark.
flow.context: This activity looks for tiny sparks of static electricity, which you can see only in the dark.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up wearing a sweater pulls it off slowly over their head. 2. Everyone watches the sweater and listens. 3. Try again, faster.
flow.say: Watch the sweater very closely, and listen. What do you hear? What do you see? Where does it come from?
flow.kid: Watch the sweater in the dark. Listen too. What do you notice?
flow.parent: On a dry night you hear crackles and may see tiny blue flashes along the wool. Synthetic sweaters and fleece often work best. In damp weather you may hear only a few crackles and see nothing. You can also rub a balloon on the sweater in the dark and bring a fingertip close to it.

ask.q: What do you think the crackle and the flash are?
good: Charge jumping across the air, like tiny lightning.

flow.do: Switch the light back on and talk.
flow.say: Each crackle was a tiny spark. How is it like lightning and thunder?
flow.kid: Each crackle was a tiny spark. How is it like lightning?

check.q: What is the crackle you hear when you pull off a sweater in the dark?
options: The wool tearing
The sound of tiny sparks heating the air, like tiny thunder
Air coming out of the wool
check.why: Rubbing gives the sweater and your shirt opposite charges. When enough builds up, charge jumps across the air in a tiny spark. The spark heats the air, which snaps outwards. That is a tiny thunder. Picking 'wool tearing' is a good guess, but the sweater is not damaged afterwards.

activities.context: In this activity you look and listen for tiny sparks of static from a sweater in a dark room. Each one is a tiny lightning flash with a tiny thunder.

activities.title: The Rolling Can

materials.item: a round balloon, blown up and tied
a woollen sweater, shawl or monkey cap, or clean dry hair
an empty aluminium drink can, or a cardboard tube from inside a foil roll wrapped in kitchen foil
a smooth floor or table

activities.safety: Pick up every piece of a popped balloon at once, because small children can choke on them. A grown-up checks the can's opening for sharp edges.

schedule.what: Lay a can on its side. Make it roll with a rubbed balloon, without touching it.

activities.record: Draw the can and the balloon, with an arrow for the way the can rolled.

flow.do: 1. Lay the empty can on its side on a smooth floor. 2. Bring a plain balloon close to it, without touching.
flow.say: Can a balloon move this can without touching it? Let's try a plain balloon first.
flow.kid: Bring a plain balloon close to the can. Does it move?
flow.context: This activity uses a rubbed balloon to roll an empty can without touching it.

flow.do: 1. Rub the balloon on wool or hair 10 times. 2. Hold the rubbed side about 3 cm in front of the can. 3. Move the balloon slowly away, keeping just ahead of the can.
flow.say: Now rub the balloon and hold it near the can. Move it slowly away. What does the can do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Rub the balloon. Hold it near the can. Move it slowly away.
flow.parent: The can rolls towards the balloon and follows it as you move away. If the balloon touches the can, some charge is lost. Rub it again. A light aluminium can works much better than a steel tin.

flow.do: 1. Make a start line and a finish line 50 cm apart with tape or chalk. 2. Race the can to the finish, using only the balloon.
flow.say: Can you roll the can all the way to the finish line, without touching it? How many times did you need to rub the balloon again?
flow.kid: Roll the can to the finish line. Don't touch it!

check.q: The can has no charge. Why does it roll towards the rubbed balloon?
options: The balloon pushes the electrons in the can to the far side, so the near side is pulled
The can is magnetic
The balloon blows air at it
check.why: The balloon's extra electrons push the electrons in the metal can to the far side. The near side is left with plus charge, and it is pulled towards the balloon. Picking 'magnetic' is a good thought, but aluminium is not magnetic, and a plain balloon does nothing.

activities.context: In this activity you roll an empty can along the floor using only a rubbed balloon.

setup.caption: 1. Lay a can on its side. Try a plain balloon.

setup.caption: 2. Rub the balloon and lead the can to the finish line.

activities.title: Our Storm Safety Plan

materials.item: paper and coloured pencils
a phone with the Damini lightning app, if a grown-up wants to install it

activities.safety: Do this on a calm day, never during a storm.

schedule.what: Walk round your home and make a plan for what to do in a thunderstorm.

activities.record: Make a poster: 'When we hear thunder, we…', with five rules and a reason for each.

flow.do: 1. Walk round your home together. 2. Find the safest room, away from big windows. 3. Find the places to avoid in a storm: the terrace or balcony, the bathroom taps, and corded appliances.
flow.say: Let's plan what we do in a thunderstorm. Where is the safest place in our home? Where should we not be? Why?
flow.kid: Walk round your home. Find the safest room. Find places to avoid.
flow.context: This activity makes a plan for staying safe in a thunderstorm, for your own home.

flow.do: 1. Make the poster together. 2. Write five rules with a reason for each. 3. Stick it near the door.
flow.say: Let's write our rules. For each rule, say why it keeps us safe.
flow.kid: Write five storm rules. Say why for each one.
flow.parent: Good rules: go inside at the first thunder, because if you can hear thunder, lightning can reach you. Stay off the terrace and balcony. No bathing or washing up during the storm, because lightning can travel along pipes. Keep away from corded appliances. Wait about 30 minutes after the last thunder before going out. The Damini app, made by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology in Pune, gives lightning warnings.

check.q: Why should you not have a bath during a thunderstorm?
options: The water gets cold
Lightning can travel along metal pipes and water into the bathroom
The noise is too loud
check.why: If lightning strikes a building, the charge can travel along metal pipes and the water in them. So taps and baths are not safe during a storm. Picking 'cold' is true some days, but it is not the danger.

activities.context: In this activity you make a thunderstorm safety plan for your own home, with a reason for every rule.

setup.art: A parent and child standing in a hallway of a flat, pointing towards the balcony door and the bathroom.
setup.caption: 1. Walk round your home and find the safe and unsafe places.

setup.caption: 2. Make a poster with five rules and a reason for each.

activities.title: Be a Storm Cloud

materials.item: paper, a red pen and a blue pen
space to move about

activities.safety: Move slowly and carefully, away from furniture.

schedule.what: Act out how ice and hail inside a storm cloud bump and build up charge until lightning jumps.

activities.record: Draw the cloud with plus at the top and minus at the bottom, and a lightning bolt.

flow.do: 1. Make a small paper sign marked plus in red, and one marked minus in blue, for each person. 2. Everyone starts in the middle of the room as a water drop.
flow.say: We are all water drops inside a storm cloud. The wind is carrying us up into the cold top of the cloud, where we freeze.
flow.kid: You are a water drop in a storm cloud. The wind lifts you up!
flow.context: This is an act-out of how a storm cloud builds up charge until lightning jumps.

flow.do: 1. Half of the players are light ice crystals and half are heavy hail. 2. Players walk about and gently bump elbows. 3. After each bump, ice crystals hold up a plus sign and move to one end of the room, the top. 4. Hail hold up a minus sign and move to the other end, the bottom.
flow.say: Ice crystals are light. When they bump the hail, they get plus charge and the wind lifts them to the top. Hail is heavy. It gets minus charge and stays near the bottom.
flow.kid: Bump elbows gently. Ice goes to the top with plus. Hail stays low with minus.
flow.parent: This is a simple picture of the main idea. Scientists still study exactly how each bump moves the charge.

flow.do: When everyone has moved, the grown-up calls 'Spark!' and everyone claps once, loudly.
flow.say: The top is full of plus and the bottom full of minus. The charge is too big. Spark! That clap is the thunder.
flow.kid: Too much charge! Spark! Clap once for the thunder.

check.q: In a storm cloud, how does the charge build up?
options: Ice crystals and hail bump into each other, and charge moves between them
The Sun charges the cloud
Rain is made of electricity
check.why: Bumps between light ice crystals and heavier hail move charge, a bit like rubbing a balloon. The light crystals carry plus to the top. Picking 'the Sun' is a fair guess, because the Sun's warmth drives the winds, but the charge comes from the bumping.

activities.context: In this act-out you are the ice and hail inside a storm cloud. You find out how the cloud builds up charge until lightning jumps.

setup.caption: 1. Be ice crystals and hail. Bump gently.

setup.art: The same children split to two ends of the room, plus signs at one end and minus at the other, all clapping as a parent calls 'Spark!'.
setup.caption: 2. Plus goes to the top, minus to the bottom. Spark!

20 small paper napkin bits on a dark plate

a notebook and pencil

schedule.what: Rub the balloon 10 times on the same wool, count the paper bits it lifts, and write down whether the air feels dry or damp.

projects.record: Make a table with a row for each day: date, dry or damp, humidity if you know it, and bits lifted. On the last day, draw a bar chart.

flow.do: 1. Rub the balloon 10 times on the wool. 2. Hold it 2 cm over the 20 bits for 3 seconds. 3. Count the bits that cling. 4. Write the count, and whether the air feels dry or sticky. 5. Add the humidity number from a weather app, if you have one.
flow.say: Every day this week we will do the same test at the same time. Does the weather change how well the balloon works? What do you think? Why?
flow.kid: Rub the balloon ten times. Count the bits. Is the air dry or damp?
flow.parent: Use the same balloon, the same wool and the same time of day. A humidity number from a weather app is a percentage: the higher it is, the damper the air. If all five days are much the same, try one day in an AC room as well.
flow.context: This is the first day of a 5-day project. You test a balloon each day and find out how the weather changes static electricity.

flow.do: Do the same test once a day for the next three days.
flow.say: Same balloon, same wool, same time. How many today? Is it a dry day or a damp day?
flow.kid: Same test again. How many bits today? Dry or damp?
flow.wait: Days 2 to 4: do the test once each day.

flow.do: 1. Do the test on the last day. 2. Draw a bar for each day. 3. Look for a pattern.
flow.say: Look at your bars. On which days did the balloon lift the most? What was the air like on those days?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each day. When did it lift the most?
flow.wait: Day 5: the last test, then draw the chart.

check.q: Meera's balloon lifted 15 bits on a dry day and 3 bits on a rainy day. What is the best reason?
options: The balloon was tired on the rainy day
Damp air lets the charge leak away through a thin layer of water
Rain makes paper heavier
check.why: In damp air, a very thin layer of water forms on the balloon, and water lets the charge leak away. Picking 'paper heavier' is a fair thought, because damp paper is a little heavier, but the main reason is the charge leaking away.

projects.context: In this 5-day project you test a rubbed balloon every day and find out how dry and damp weather change static electricity.

challenges.title: The Can Race: how far can a balloon pull?
challenges.problem: Roll an empty can 1 metre along the floor using only rubbed balloons, as quickly as you can, without touching the can. Find the best way to keep the balloon charged.
constraints: Use only balloons, cloths and things from home.
Time each try, and change only one thing between tries.
materials: an empty aluminium drink can, or a foil-wrapped cardboard tube
wool, a cotton towel and other cloths to test
tape for a start and finish line
a phone timer or a clock with a seconds hand
general: Rub the balloon well, hold it close in front of the can, and walk backwards slowly.
Rub again whenever the can slows down.
creative: Use two balloons, one rubbed while the other pulls, and swap.
Try a rubbed plastic ruler or a big plastic sheet instead of a balloon.
Find the smoothest floor in your home for the race.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way to win the Can Race. Draw your plan, test it, and beat your best time.

flow.do: 1. Mark a start and a finish 1 metre apart. 2. Look at the problem together and draw two ideas.
flow.say: We need the can to cross the line, and nothing can touch it. What makes the balloon pull best? Let's draw two ideas.
flow.kid: Draw two ideas to roll the can to the finish.
flow.context: This is an engineering challenge. You find the fastest way to roll a can with static electricity.

flow.do: 1. Try your first idea and time it. 2. Change one thing, such as the cloth or how close you hold the balloon. 3. Time it again.
flow.say: Try it and time it. Now change just one thing. Was it faster?
flow.kid: Try it. Time it. Change one thing. Try again!
flow.parent: Holding the balloon close, without touching, makes the biggest difference, because the force gets much stronger closer up. A touch takes away charge, so the balloon then needs rubbing again.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative ideas together.
flow.say: Here are some other ideas. Which one would you try next? Can you invent a better one?
flow.kid: Read the other ideas. Can you invent a better one?

check.q: Why does the can slow down if the balloon touches it?
options: The touch takes some charge off the balloon
The can gets heavier
The balloon gets colder
check.why: The can is metal, a conductor. When the balloon touches it, some of the balloon's extra electrons move onto the can, so the balloon has less charge to pull with. Picking 'heavier' does not fit, because nothing is added to the can that you could weigh.

challenges.title: Build a Charge Detector
challenges.problem: Build a detector that shows when something is charged, even when it is too weak to lift paper. Two thin strips of foil inside a jar must spread apart when a charged thing comes near.
constraints: The foil strips must be inside a jar, out of the wind.
Nothing charged may touch the strips themselves.
materials: a piece of thick cardboard bigger than the jar's mouth
the thinnest foil you have, such as a chocolate wrapper or kitchen foil
general: Push the straightened paper clip through the middle of the cardboard. Bend its bottom end into a hook. Hang two strips of foil, each about 1 cm by 4 cm, side by side on the hook. Put the cardboard on the jar with the strips hanging inside. Press a small foil ball onto the top of the clip.
Bring a rubbed balloon near the foil ball, without touching it. The strips should spread apart.
creative: Test which cloths charge the balloon most by how far the strips spread.
Test a rubbed comb, a rubbed ruler and a rubbed steel spoon.
Find out whether your hair is still charged a minute after you rub it.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own charge detector, or improve this one so the strips spread further. Draw it, build it and test it.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pushes the paper clip through the cardboard. 2. Bend a hook at the bottom. 3. Hang the two foil strips on the hook. 4. Put the cardboard on the jar. 5. Put the foil ball on top.
flow.say: We are making a detector. The charge will travel down the metal clip into the two foil strips. Then what do you think the strips will do?
flow.kid: Build the detector. Hang two foil strips on the clip inside the jar.
flow.parent: The thinner and lighter the foil, the better it works. Chocolate wrapper foil often works better than kitchen foil. The strips must hang freely and touch each other at the start.
flow.context: This is an engineering challenge. You build a jar that shows when something is charged.

flow.do: 1. Rub the balloon on wool 10 times. 2. Bring it slowly towards the foil ball, without touching. 3. Watch the strips. 4. Take the balloon away.
flow.say: Bring the rubbed balloon slowly closer. Watch the strips. What happens? And when I take it away?
flow.kid: Bring the rubbed balloon close. Don't touch. Watch the strips!
flow.parent: The strips spread apart as the balloon comes near, and fall back together when it goes. The balloon pushes electrons down the clip into both strips, so both strips get the same charge, and they repel. On a damp day the movement is small, so try it in an AC room.

flow.do: Try the creative ideas and talk about why it works.
flow.say: Why do the two strips push apart? What charge do they both have?
flow.kid: Why do the two strips push apart?

check.q: Why do the two foil strips spread apart when a rubbed balloon comes near?
options: Both strips get the same kind of charge, and the same charges repel
The balloon blows them apart
The strips get warm
check.why: The balloon's extra electrons push electrons along the metal clip down into both strips. Both strips now have extra minus charge, and the same charges repel. Picking 'blows them apart' is a fair guess, but the strips are inside a covered jar, away from any air.
