quiz.p: A new balloon, straight out of the packet, does not lift paper bits. Why not?
opts: It has no charge in it at all
It has equal plus and minus charge, so they cancel
quiz.why: Every atom in the balloon has plus and minus charge, in equal amounts, so they cancel. We call it neutral. Picking 'no charge at all' is a very common idea, but the balloon is full of charge. It is only balanced.

quiz.p: Swathi rubs a balloon on her dry hair. Electrons move from her hair onto the balloon. What charge does her hair have now?
quiz.why: Her hair has lost some electrons, which are minus, so it is left with extra plus charge. Picking 'minus' mixes up the two: the balloon gained the electrons, so the balloon is the one with extra minus.

quiz.p: Two balloons are both rubbed on wool and hung side by side on threads. What do they do?
quiz.why: Both balloons got the same kind of charge from the wool, and the same charges repel. Picking 'towards each other' would be right only if they had opposite charges.

quiz.p: After rubbing with a balloon, Anjali's hair stands up and the strands spread apart. Why do the strands spread apart?
opts: Each strand has the same plus charge, and the same charges repel
The strands are pulled by gravity
quiz.why: Every strand lost electrons to the balloon, so every strand has plus charge. The same charges push each other away. Gravity pulls the hair down, not apart.

quiz.p: A rubbed comb bends a thin stream of tap water. The water was never rubbed. Why does it bend?
opts: The water is charged by the tap
The comb's charge pushes the water's electrons a tiny way, so the near side is pulled
The comb blows on the water
quiz.why: The water is neutral. The comb's charge moves the electrons in the water a tiny way, so the side nearest the comb gets the opposite charge and is pulled. Picking 'charged by the tap' is a fair guess, but the stream does not bend at all until the comb comes near.

quiz.p: In the Rubbing Test, Fathima rubbed a balloon with five things. Which result shows that rubbing two of the same material moves hardly any charge?
quiz.why: Two balloons are the same material, so neither grabs electrons harder, and the balloon lifted nothing. Picking cotton is close, because cotton charged it only a little, but cotton is a different material from rubber.

quiz.p: Why do we test the balloon over the paper before rubbing it at all?
opts: To see what happens with no rubbing, so we can compare
quiz.why: A test with no rubbing shows that the balloon on its own lifts nothing. Then we know that any bits it lifts later are because of the rubbing. Scientists call this a control.

quiz.p: Balloon tricks that worked in Bengaluru in January do not work in Kochi in the monsoon. Why?
opts: The damp air leaves a thin layer of water that lets the charge leak away
It is too hot for electrons
quiz.why: Water lets charge move. In humid air, a thin layer of water on the balloon lets its extra electrons leak away. Picking 'too hot' is a fair thought, but the dampness is what matters: a dry hot day works well.

quiz.p: Lalitha rubs a steel spoon on wool, holding its handle. It does not bend the water stream. Why?
opts: Steel is a conductor, so the charge runs through the spoon and her body
She did not rub it enough
quiz.why: Steel and your body are conductors, so any charge on the spoon runs away through her hand. Plastic is an insulator, so a comb keeps its charge.

opts: A giant spark of electric charge jumping from a storm cloud
quiz.why: Lightning is a giant spark, the same kind of thing as the tiny crackle from a sweater, only far bigger. Picking 'fire' is how many people once thought of it, but it is electric charge heating the air.

quiz.p: Why do you hear thunder after you see the lightning?
opts: Light travels much faster than sound
quiz.why: The flash and the bang happen together. Light reaches you almost at once, but sound takes about 3 seconds to travel 1 kilometre. Picking 'made later' is a natural guess, but the hot air bursts outwards at the same moment as the flash.

quiz.p: You are playing in a park when you hear thunder. What should you do?
opts: Go inside a building at once
quiz.why: If you can hear thunder, lightning is close enough to reach you. A building is safe. A lone tree is one of the most dangerous places, because lightning often strikes tall things.

quiz.p: Why is a closed car a safe place in a thunderstorm?
opts: Its rubber tyres stop the lightning
Its metal body carries the charge round the outside to the ground
quiz.why: The metal body carries the charge around you and into the ground. Picking 'tyres' is the most common belief, but a few centimetres of rubber cannot stop a spark that has crossed kilometres of air.

quiz.p: In 1752, what did Thomas-François Dalibard's helper in France get from a tall iron rod during a storm?
quiz.why: Sparks jumped from the iron rod, which showed that storm clouds are electrically charged and that lightning is electricity. Benjamin Franklin had suggested the test.

items.p: The tiny particles with minus charge that move when you rub a balloon are called ____.
items.why: Electrons are in the outer part of every atom, and they are the part that can be rubbed off.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: a material that keeps charge where it is put
a material that lets charge move through it
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These five words come up all through the unit.

items.p: Sort these pairs. Do they attract or repel?
items: a plus charge and a minus charge
a rubbed balloon and a paper bit
a rubbed balloon and your rubbed hair
items.a: see items
items.why: Opposites attract and the same charges repel. A charged thing also attracts a neutral thing, like a paper bit.

items.p: A balloon that has not been rubbed has no electric charge inside it at all.
items.why: False. It is full of plus and minus charge, in equal amounts, so they cancel. It is neutral, not empty.

items.p: Kavitha rubs only one side of a balloon on wool. She holds the other side over paper bits. What happens?
items.why: Rubber is an insulator, so the charge stays on the patch that was rubbed. The other side has hardly any. That is why it is called static.

items.p: In the Rubbing Test, which thing made your balloon lift the most paper bits? Write what you think, what you saw, and why.
items.a: A strong answer names the winner and the number, for example: wool lifted 12 bits and cotton only 3. It says that rubbing moves electrons, and that wool gives its electrons away easily to the balloon.
items.why: This is claim, evidence and reasoning, using the child's own results.

items.p: Draw a balloon over your head, just after you rubbed it on your hair. Put minus signs where the extra electrons are, and plus signs where electrons are missing. Draw arrows to show the pulls and pushes.
items.a: Minus signs on the rubbed side of the balloon. Plus signs on the hairs. Arrows from the hairs up towards the balloon, and small arrows between the hairs pointing apart.
items.why: A strong drawing shows both rules: opposites attract, so the hair rises, and the same charges repel, so the hairs spread.
items.art: An outline of a child's head with an empty balloon shape above it.

items.p: Which is the best place in your home to do static tricks on a sticky monsoon day?
opts: The bathroom after a hot bath
A room with the AC running
items.why: An AC takes water out of the air, so the charge leaks away more slowly. The bathroom and the balcony are full of damp air.

items.p: Lightning is the same kind of thing as the crackle you hear when you pull off a sweater, only much bigger.
items.why: True. Both are sparks: charge jumping across air and heating it, which makes light and sound.

items.p: Put these in order, to tell how lightning happens.
items: Ice crystals and hail bump into each other
Wind carries water drops up into the cold top of the cloud
Plus charge gathers at the top and minus near the bottom
a: Wind carries water drops up into the cold top of the cloud
Ice crystals and hail bump into each other
Plus charge gathers at the top and minus near the bottom
items.why: The water must freeze, then the bumps move charge, then the charge separates, and only when it is big enough does the spark jump.

items.p: Sort these. Is each one safe or unsafe in a thunderstorm?
items: inside a building with the door shut
sitting in a room away from taps
items.a: see items
items.why: Buildings and closed cars give the charge a path around you. Tall lone things, water and kite strings can bring lightning to you.

items.p: Your little cousin wants to stand under a big tree in a field to keep dry in a thunderstorm. What would you tell him, and why?
items.a: Tell him not to, because lightning often strikes tall things standing alone, like a tree, and the lightning can jump to a person sheltering below. He should go inside a building at once.
items.why: A strong answer gives the rule and the reason.

items.p: Things that let charge move easily, like metals and water, are called ____.
items.why: Conductors let charge move. That is why a steel spoon does not stay charged in your hand.

items.p: The plastic strips of a rubbed tassel spread out like a fan. What does this show?
opts: The strips have the same kind of charge, and the same charges repel
items.why: All the strips were rubbed with the same wool, so they got the same kind of charge, and they push each other away.

items.p: Write one question you still have about static electricity or lightning, and say how you might find out the answer.
items.a: Any real question with a way to find out. For example: does a plastic spoon charge as well as a comb? I could test both over the water stream.
items.why: A strong answer asks something that can be tested, and says what the test would be.

items.p: Nandini and her brother Vikram watch paper bits jump up to a rubbed balloon. They disagree about why.

views.says: The paper must be charged too, with the opposite charge. Only opposite charges attract.
The paper is not charged. The balloon is charged, and that is enough to pull the paper.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give your evidence. Then say what the other person got right.
items.a: A strong answer sides mostly with Vikram: the paper was never rubbed, and it is neutral. But it gives Nandini her due: the near side of the paper does get a little opposite charge, because the balloon pushes the paper's electrons a tiny way back. So both are partly right.
items.why: This tests the hardest idea in the unit: how a charged thing attracts a neutral one.

items.p: Ranjini rubs a balloon on her hair. The balloon now has 1,000 extra electrons. How many electrons has her hair lost?
items.why: Rubbing does not make or destroy charge. Every electron the balloon gained came from her hair, so her hair lost exactly 1,000. Real numbers are far bigger, but the rule is the same.

items.p: Arun says, 'Rubbing a balloon makes electricity.' Use what you saw in this unit to explain what rubbing really does.
items.a: Rubbing does not make charge. It moves electrons from one thing to the other. The balloon gets extra minus charge, and the hair is left with the same amount of plus. My hair rose to the balloon, which shows the hair was charged too.
items.why: A strong answer corrects the idea and uses the rising hair as evidence that both things got charged.

items.p: A steel spoon can never be charged at all.
items.why: False. Steel can carry charge, but held in your hand, the charge runs away through the steel and through your body. A steel spoon on a plastic stand, not touched, can hold charge for a while.

items.p: A rubbed comb touches the water stream for a moment. Afterwards it hardly bends the water. Why?
opts: The comb is now wet, and the water lets the charge leak away
The water washed off the plastic
items.why: Water is a conductor, so a wet comb loses its charge. Dry it and rub it again, and it works.

items.p: Draw a paper bit just below a rubbed balloon. Inside the paper, draw where the plus and minus charges move. Draw an arrow to show which way the paper moves.
items.a: Minus on the balloon. Plus signs crowded on the top of the paper, near the balloon, and minus signs on the bottom. An arrow pointing up.
items.why: The near side of the paper gets the opposite charge and is pulled more strongly than the far side is pushed.
items.art: A balloon shape with an empty square of paper below it.

items.p: Why does a charged balloon lift a paper bit but not a book?
opts: The electric force is small, so it can only lift very light things
items.why: The force on a neutral thing is small, so it lifts only very light things like paper bits, pepper and hair. A book is far heavier.

items.p: Put these in order, from the one that charged the balloon most to least, using these made-up results: cotton 3 bits, wool 12 bits, newspaper 5 bits, dry hair 14 bits.
items.why: More bits lifted means more charge. Dry hair 14, wool 12, newspaper 5 and cotton 3.

items.p: In the Static Weather Diary, Deepa's balloon lifted 15 bits on Monday and only 2 bits on Thursday. Suggest a reason, and say how she could check it.
items.a: Thursday was probably a damper day, so the charge leaked away. She could check the humidity in a weather app for each day, or test on a damp day in an AC room to see if the count goes up.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason from the science and a test that could show whether it is right.

items.p: The sound made when lightning heats the air so fast that it bursts outwards is called ____.
items.why: Thunder is the sound of air heated by lightning to nearly 30,000 degrees Celsius.

items.p: You see a lightning flash. You count 6 seconds before you hear the thunder. About how far away was it?
items.why: Sound travels about 1 kilometre in 3 seconds. 6 seconds divided by 3 is 2, so about 2 kilometres. That is close enough to be dangerous.

items.p: Sort these materials. Does each one keep its charge in your hand, or let it run away?
items.a: see items
items.why: Insulators like plastic and rubber keep the charge where it is put. Conductors like metals and water let it run away through your body.

items.p: A bumblebee flies to a flower that another bee visited a few seconds ago. How can the bee tell?
opts: The flower's electric field has changed for a while
The flower tells her with a sound
The bee can see the nectar is gone
items.why: When a charged bee lands, the flower's electric field changes for a while. Bumblebees can feel this with the tiny hairs on their body, and skip that flower, which saves them time.

items.p: Why is it dangerous to fly a kite when a storm is coming? Use the words conductor and lightning.
items.a: A kite flies high, and its string can get wet. A wet string is a conductor, so lightning could travel down it into the person holding it.
items.why: A strong answer joins the height of the kite to the conductor idea.

items.p: Draw a storm cloud. Show where the plus charge gathers, where the minus charge gathers, and a lightning bolt to the ground.
items.a: Plus signs at the top of the cloud, minus signs near the bottom, and a bolt from the bottom of the cloud down to the ground.
items.why: Light ice crystals carry plus to the top, and heavy hail keeps minus lower down. The bottom attracts plus charge on the ground below.
items.art: An empty outline of a tall cloud above flat ground.

items.p: In the 1700s, people argued about how to protect a tall building from lightning.

views.who: Benjamin Franklin, a scientist in America
views.says: Put a pointed iron rod on top, joined by a metal strip to the ground. The charge will flow down the strip, not through the building.

views.who: Many church leaders of the time
views.says: Ring the church bells loudly during a storm. The sound will drive the lightning away.
A rod is a good idea, but it might attract more lightning than there would be without it.

items.ask: Which idea would you choose for your own building? Give your evidence. Then say what the strongest point of another view is.
items.a: A strong answer chooses Franklin's rod, because a metal strip is a conductor and gives the charge an easy path to the ground. It may say that bells were in tall towers, which lightning often struck, so ringing them put the ringers in danger. It gives the third view its due: a rod does not stop lightning, it only guides it safely, which is why the strip to the ground matters.
items.why: This uses the ideas of conductors and tall things in a real old argument.

items.p: Indira rubs a balloon on a woollen shawl and a second balloon on her hair. She hangs them side by side, and they lean apart. What does this tell her?
opts: Both balloons got the same kind of charge
items.why: The balloons repel, so they must have the same kind of charge. Both took electrons, from the wool and from the hair.

items.p: Your hair is a conductor when it is wet, but your hair can stay charged after a balloon. Explain how both can be true.
items.a: Dry hair is a poor conductor, almost an insulator, so the charge stays on it for a while. Wet hair has water on it, and water is a conductor, so wet hair loses its charge quickly. That is why static tricks need dry hair.
items.why: A strong answer sees that whether something holds charge depends on whether it is dry.

items.p: Why does a can roll towards a rubbed balloon even more easily than a paper bit of the same weight?
opts: The can is metal, so its electrons can move all the way to the far side
items.why: In metal, electrons move freely, so the balloon pushes many of them right to the far side of the can. The near side gets a big plus charge and a strong pull. In paper, electrons can move only a tiny way.

items.p: Draw the charge detector jar with a rubbed balloon held near its foil ball. Show where the extra electrons go, and what the two foil strips do.
items.a: Minus on the balloon. Electrons pushed down the clip into the strips, so both strips have minus signs and spread apart in a V. The foil ball at the top has plus signs.
items.why: This shows charges moving through a conductor, and the same charges repelling.
items.art: An empty outline of a glass jar with a lid and a paper clip.

items.p: A tall building with a lightning conductor will never be struck by lightning.
items.why: False. The rod may still be struck, but the charge flows down the metal strip into the ground instead of through the building, so the building is not harmed.

items.p: Lightning flashes about 45 times every second somewhere on Earth. About how many flashes is that in one minute?
items.why: One minute is 60 seconds. 45 times 60 is 2,700.

items.p: Many people say lightning never strikes the same place twice. Plan a way you could check this, using real records.
items.a: Look up the records of how often one tall building or tower is struck, for example the Empire State Building, which is struck about 20 to 25 times a year. If a place is struck more than once, the saying is wrong.
items.why: A strong answer uses records as evidence instead of a feeling.

items.p: Put these in order, from the weakest spark to the strongest.
items: a static shock from a car door
a: a static shock from a car door
items.why: All three are sparks of static charge. A sweater crackle is tiny, a car door shock is a little bigger and stings, and lightning carries millions of times more.

items.p: A young spider has no wings but needs to travel to a new home. How does the Earth's electric field help?
opts: It pulls on the spider's charged silk threads and helps lift the spider into the air
items.why: The spider lets out silk threads that carry charge. The Earth's electric field pulls on them and helps lift the spider up, so they can drift to a new place. This is called ballooning.

items.p: An atom with 8 protons and 8 electrons has an overall charge of ____.
items.why: 8 plus charges and 8 minus charges cancel, so the overall charge is zero. The atom is neutral.

items.p: Your hair rose up to a balloon against the pull of the whole Earth. What does that tell you about how strong the electric force is, compared with gravity?
items.a: The electric force from a small balloon beat the pull of the whole Earth on the hair. So the electric force must be very strong. We do not notice it most of the time because plus and minus usually cancel.
items.why: A strong answer compares the two forces using the rising hair as evidence, and explains why we rarely notice the electric force.

items.p: Why does a closed car protect you from lightning, but an open scooter does not?
opts: A car's metal body carries the charge around you to the ground, and a scooter has no metal shell around you
items.why: The car's metal shell is a conductor around you. On a scooter, nothing surrounds you, so you can be the path to the ground.

items.p: Design a poster for your building's lift: 'What to do in a thunderstorm'. Show four rules with a picture for each.
items.a: Four clear rules with pictures, for example: go inside at the first thunder, stay off the terrace, no baths or washing up during the storm, wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.
items.why: A strong poster gives rules that really keep people safe, each with a reason a neighbour would understand.

items.p: Nobody knows exactly how the very first spark of a lightning bolt starts. Why do you think it is hard to find out?
items.a: Any sensible reason. For example: lightning starts high inside a storm cloud, it is over in a fraction of a second, and it is dangerous to fly instruments into a storm.
items.why: This is an open question in science. A strong answer thinks about what makes it hard to measure.

applications: Photocopiers and laser printers use static charge to make black toner powder stick to paper in the shape of the words.
Factory chimneys use charged plates to catch smoke and dust before it reaches the air.
Car factories give paint drops a charge, so the paint is pulled evenly onto the car body and less is wasted.
Lightning conductors protect tall buildings, towers and temples.
Petrol tankers are joined to the ground with a wire before they unload, so no spark can jump near the fuel.
Cling film sticks to bowls partly because of static charge.
Electronics workers wear a strap joined to the ground, so a static spark from their body does not damage a computer chip.
Weather services track lightning with sensors and satellites to warn people, as the Damini app does in India.

open_questions.q: How does a lightning bolt start?
open_questions.why_open: The charge measured inside storm clouds seems too weak to tear the air and start a spark. Some scientists think tiny particles from space, called cosmic rays, may help. Nobody knows for sure.

open_questions.q: Why does rubbing two materials move electrons one way and not the other?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can list which materials usually gain electrons and which lose them, but the list does not always hold. Even two pieces of the same material can charge each other. Nobody yet fully understands why.

open_questions.q: What exactly happens to the charge in each bump between ice and hail in a cloud?
open_questions.why_open: Laboratory tests show the bumps move charge, but which piece gets plus depends on temperature, water and speed, in ways that are still being worked out.

open_questions.q: How many animals can sense electric fields in the air?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists found that bumblebees can sense them only in 2013, and spiders in 2018. Many other insects have not been tested yet.

maths.problem: In the Rubbing Test, Fathima's balloon lifted these paper bits: dry hair 14, wool 12, newspaper 5, cotton 3, another balloon 0. How many more bits did hair lift than cotton? How many bits were lifted in all?
maths.answer: Hair lifted 11 more than cotton. 34 bits were lifted in all.
maths.context: This is about the Rubbing Test, where you rub a balloon with different things and count the paper bits it lifts.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the counts shows which material gave the most charge, and by how much.

maths.problem: Sound travels about 1 kilometre in 3 seconds. Gayathri counts 12 seconds between a flash of lightning and the thunder. About how far away was the lightning?
maths.explain: Every 3 seconds is about 1 kilometre. 12 divided by 3 is 4. So the lightning was about 4 kilometres away.
maths.context: This is about thunder, which you hear after the flash because sound is slower than light.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the seconds by 3 turns a count you can make into a distance you cannot measure.

maths.problem: Lightning flashes about 45 times every second somewhere on Earth. How many flashes is that in 10 seconds? In one minute?
maths.answer: About 450 in 10 seconds, and about 2,700 in a minute.
maths.explain: 45 times 10 is 450. One minute is 60 seconds, which is 6 lots of 10 seconds. 450 times 6 is 2,700.
maths.context: This is about how often lightning flashes on the whole Earth.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how common lightning really is, though most of us see it only a few times a year.

maths.problem: In her Static Weather Diary, Meera's balloon lifted 15, 13, 4, 2 and 14 bits on five days. On two of the days it rained. Which two days were probably the rainy ones? Why?
maths.explain: Damp air lets charge leak away, so a rainy day gives a low count. The counts 4 and 2 are much lower than the others, which are all 13 or more.
maths.context: This is about the Static Weather Diary, where you test a balloon each day and note the weather.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the odd results in a list lets you match them to a cause.

maths.problem: Lightning can heat the air to about 30,000 degrees Celsius. The surface of the Sun is about 6,000 degrees Celsius. About how many times hotter is lightning?
maths.explain: How many 6,000s make 30,000? 6,000 times 5 is 30,000. So lightning is about 5 times as hot as the Sun's surface.
maths.context: This is about how hot lightning makes the air in its path.
maths.why_maths: Comparing with the Sun gives a feel for a number too big to imagine.

roots.context: We have rubbed balloons, bent water and learned what lightning is. Now we ask what static electricity tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your hair and the balloon were each full of plus and minus charge, in equal amounts. Rubbing moved only a tiny share of the electrons from your hair to the balloon. Yet that small imbalance lifted your hair against the pull of the whole Earth. So the electric force is huge, and it hides only because charges almost always balance.
deep_truth.habit: We think of things as either electric or not electric, and of a plain balloon as having no electricity in it. But every object is packed with charge. What we call 'no charge' is a very exact balance of plus and minus.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Rubbing Test, the plain balloon lifted no paper at all. After only ten rubs, the same balloon lifted paper bits, and your hair rose up towards it, against gravity.

three.who_am_i: You are made of countless plus and minus charges, held in balance. That balance holds every atom of you together.
three.what_is_life: A bee feels the faint electric field of a flower, and uses it to choose which flower to visit.
three.what_is_this_world: The same force that lifts a paper bit builds the lightning in a monsoon storm.

roots.thread: A plain balloon looks as if nothing is going on inside it. In fact it holds huge amounts of plus and minus charge, which add up to exactly zero. Tip that balance a tiny way, by rubbing, and forces appear at once: hair rises, paper jumps, water bends and sparks crackle. In a storm cloud, the same tipping, on a giant scale, makes lightning. Out of one quiet balance come many different happenings.

teachings.teaching: All things carry the dark, yin, on their back and hold the light, yang, in their arms. Blending the two, they reach harmony.
teachings.link: Every atom holds plus and minus together, and their balance is what makes an ordinary, quiet object. Your balloon showed what happens when that balance is upset a little.

teachings.teaching: The hymn tells how Indra struck the serpent Vritra with his thunderbolt, the vajra, and set free the waters held back in the clouds.
teachings.link: People who wrote this hymn saw that lightning and rain come together. Science agrees that lightning is made in tall rain clouds, by the bumping ice and water that also bring the rain. It explains the link with charge instead of with a god.

science.text: Electric charge is never made or destroyed. Rubbing only moves it from one thing to another.
The electric force between two electrons is far, far stronger than the pull of gravity between them.
Exactly how the first spark of a lightning bolt starts inside a cloud is not yet known.

other_view.view: Plus and minus are only names that Benjamin Franklin chose, and their balance is a plain fact about particles. Comparing it with yin and yang, or with a god's thunderbolt, is a nice picture, but it tells us nothing new about the balloon.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home, with the materials listed. The biggest risk is damp air: static works badly in humid weather, so every step says what to do, and an AC room is suggested because an AC dries the air. Bend the Water works on more days than the balloon tests, so it is offered as the fallback. Oiled hair often charges badly, so wool is always given as the other choice. To take the charge off between tries in the Rubbing Test, the balloon is patted with a damp hand and then checked over the paper, because wiping it dry could charge it again. Paper bits come from a paper napkin peeled into one layer, which is light enough to jump. The two balloons rubbed together usually lift very few bits, but not always none, so the steps say 'usually'. The steel spoon does not bend the water when held in the hand, because the charge runs away through the body. The charge detector may move only a little with kitchen foil, so the thinnest foil is asked for. Sparks in the Dark depends on a dry night, and the steps say so. Lightning is never experimented with: it is only explained, acted out and planned for. The spine is the sticky balloon, the Rubbing Test, the explanation cards, roots and the quiz, about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1700s, people could make small sparks by rubbing glass tubes. Some wondered whether lightning was the same thing, only bigger. Many others thought it was something quite different, and in many towns church bells were rung during storms to drive lightning away. In 1750, Benjamin Franklin, a printer and scientist in Philadelphia in America, suggested a test. Put a tall iron rod on high ground, standing on something that does not conduct, and see whether a passing storm cloud charges it. In France, Thomas-François Dalibard read Franklin's idea and set up a tall iron rod in a garden at Marly-la-Ville, near Paris. On 10 May 1752, while Dalibard was away, a storm passed over. His helper brought a wire close to the rod, and sparks jumped across with a crackle, just like the sparks from rubbed glass. Lightning was electricity. Franklin later wrote that he had done a similar test with a kite, though some historians doubt the details. In 1753, Georg Richmann was killed by lightning in St Petersburg while doing a test like this, so nobody should ever try it. Franklin's idea became the lightning conductor, which slowly replaced bell ringing as protection.
how_we_found_out.who: Benjamin Franklin, a printer and scientist in Philadelphia, and Thomas-François Dalibard, a scientist in France
how_we_found_out.when: 1750 (Franklin's proposal) and 10 May 1752 (the sparks at Marly-la-Ville)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many people thought lightning was a different thing from the small sparks of rubbed glass, and that ringing church bells would keep it away. The sparks drawn from the iron rod showed that lightning is electricity, and lightning conductors protected buildings where bells had not.
